column1: # rows.tsv -- the declared bench table. Tab-separated, "#" starts a comment.
# capture and restore-at use prepare=reset rather than prepare=dirty because both
# verbs are capture-first: a measured run of either one appends a snapshot to the
# very chain the axis is varying. Without restoring the chain ref (and its id
# index) before every timed run, the fixture would drift under the measurement --
# n would silently grow across warmup and timed runs alike. The same is true of
# jj's own snapshot-on-every-command behavior, so its capture-ish rows use
# prepare=reset too, restored via `jj op restore` instead of a git ref.
# A `-` git or jj column means the tool has no honest equivalent for that row,
# not that measuring it was skipped by accident.
# --no-optional-locks on the git read rows keeps git from writing index lock
# files mid-measurement, same reason scripts/bench.sh uses it.
# git has no automatically-recorded working-tree state at all, so chain-depth
# has nothing for it to grow: every git column on that axis is measured once,
# at the largest point only, as a reference number for what the operation
# costs in git at all -- never a claim about scaling. run.sh enforces that
# restriction; report.py's single-point verdict and the per-n dashes in the
# table are what keep a reader from misreading it as a tested chain.
# capture's jj column is `status`, not a typo: jj has no dedicated "record
# the working copy" verb, but every command snapshots it as a side effect,
# and `jj status` is the cheapest command that does. In git, capture is the
# usual stage-and-commit.
# No `undo` row in this version: `ff undo` and `jj undo` both mutate
# repository state, and an O(1) prepare that undoes that mutation before
# every timed run is a design problem of its own, separate from this suite.
# Leaving it out is a decision, not an oversight.

# No `commit` row either, for the same reason: `ff commit` mutates repository state (advances HEAD), and an O(1) prepare that undoes that before every timed run hits the same unsolved problem left open for `undo` above. The `capture` row plus the `history-depth` axis already cover the ground bench.sh's `ff commit` row measured.
# What "expect" may say: "flat" is the gate -- the row must not grow with
# its axis. "linear" is a row allowed to scale with its axis, recorded so a
# worse-than-linear turn is visible. "report" is a row measured purely for
# comparison, on an axis that is not enforcement -- the real-history rows
# below. Only "flat" ever fails a run (report.py's EXPECT_VALUES).
# real-history's log row uses a shorter git format (hash/abbrev/subject
# only, no author/date fields) than chain-depth's and history-depth's log
# rows above -- intentional, not a typo; a real repo's commit metadata isn't
# needed for this axis's comparison.

# file-count's rows are all "linear", not "flat": scanning n files costs O(n) for fufu and for git alike, so nothing on this axis is gated. What it buys is honest ff-vs-git-vs-jj comparison numbers at a realistic tree size, plus visibility if something ever goes worse than linear -- a reader can see that in the consecutive-point ratios report.py already prints, even though nothing here fails a run.
# switch and park-arrive measure a round trip (switch away, then back), not a single leg: a single leg is not self-inverse, and undoing it would need an O(n) prepare, while the round trip needs none.
# noop's ff column is the bare capture on a tree the chain already matches exactly -- the scan proves emptiness and nothing else runs, the tier-1 case from bench.sh.

# first-capture uses a new prepare kind, `fresh` (see gen_prepare in run.sh): the tree is fully untracked, and the whole point of the row is the cost of a first capture -- there is no way to measure that repeatedly without restoring "never captured" before every run.
